d: Commonly used or practiced; usual
ety: From Middle English woonted (“usual, customary”), from wont (“custom, habit, practice”), alteration of wone (“custom, habit, practice”), from Old English wuna (“custom, habit, practice; usual, wonted”), from Proto-Germanic *wunô (“custom, practice”), from Proto-Indo-European *wenh₁- (“to wish, love”). Cognate with Old Frisian wona, wuna (“custom”), Old High German giwona (“custom”). More at wont,
s: 2008 (tr.?), Lodovico Ariosto, Orlando Furioso But not with wonted welcome;—inly moved …

d: An automatic signal (usually a sound) warning of danger
ety: From Middle English alarom, from Old Italian all'arme (“to arms, to the weapons”), from Latin arma, armorum (“weapons”).
s: Just another forum, then, sounding the usual alarums on the looming threat from global warming?

d: Affectedly modest or shy especially in a playful or provocative way
ety: Inherited from Middle English demure, demwre, an abbreviation of Anglo-Norman de mure port (“with a mature demeanor”) (compare Old French meur from Latin mātūrus): *si il seyt coy e de mure port (Amur curteiz) (“he sits quietly and with a mature appearance”) * Documents illustrating the history of Scotland, CLV, 1306, Orders for the custody of Scottish prisoners, CLV: …et que eles soient de bon et
s: Miss Lizzy, I have no doubt, would be as demure and coquettish, as if ten winters more had gone over her head.

d: Mix or blend
ety: From com- + mingle.
s: This vibrant stir-fry from Christian Reynoso is Chifa cooking — the cuisine that commingles Chinese and Peruvian elements — and it’s utterly delicious.

d: Behave well or properly
ety: From late Middle English comporten, from Old French comporter, from Latin comportare (“to bring together”), from com- (“together”) + portare (“to carry”).
s: She comported herself with grace.

d: A long overcoat with a hood that can be pulled over the head
ety: Borrowed from French capote. Doublet of capot and kaput.
s: Tied round her head with a large bow and flying blue ribbons under the chin, was a fragile flat Capote like a baby’s bonnet, which allowed her hair to escape in front and her great chignon behind.

d: An ancient Egyptian mud-brick tomb with a rectangular base and sloping sides and flat roof
ety: Borrowed from Arabic مَصْطَبَة (maṣṭaba).
s: The pyramids at Giza are flanked by large cemeteries containing hundreds of mastabas.

d: A diplomatic representative of the Pope having ambassadorial status
ety: From Spanish nuncio, from Latin nūntius (“envoy”).
s: Seeing as the meeting happened at the nunciature in Washington, it could only have happened with the approval and participation of the nuncio, Archbishop Carlo Maria Vigano.

d: Someone who fights for a cause
ety: Borrowed from French paladin, from Italian paladino, from Late Latin palātīnus (“palace officer”), derived from palātium (“palace”). Doublet of palatine.
s: Below are the results of a multi-actor simulation containing a bunch of paladins with slightly different L75 and L100 talents.

d: Uncannily or threateningly dark or obscure
ety: Coined by Irish poet Mary Tighe in 1805, likely as an extension of the adverbial sense, and popularized by John Keats.
s: And we are here as on a darkling plain Swept with confused alarms of struggle and flight, Where ignorant armies clash by night

d: Marked by extreme intensity of emotions or convictions; inclined to react violently; fervid
ety: Borrowed from Middle French vehement (modern French véhément; compare Italian veemente, Portuguese veemente, Spanish vehemente); or from Latin vehemēns (“vehement; very eager; ardent, furious, impetuous; emphatic”), probably from vē- (“lacking, too little”) + mēns (“mind; intellect; judgment, reasoning”).
s: The man made a vehement display of contempt.

d: Take the place or move into the position of
ety: From Middle English supplanten, supplaunten, from Old French supplanter, from Latin supplantō (“trip up”), from sub (“from below, under”) + planta (“sole”).
s: Will online dictionaries ever supplant paper dictionaries?

d: A shout to attract attention
ety: From Middle English hallow (“pursue, urge on”), from Old French haloer, which is imitative.
s: List, list, I hear Som far off hallow break the silent Air.

d: Conspicuously and offensively loud; given to vehement outcry
ety: From Latin vōcifer + -ous.
s: Not even the most vociferous advocates of reform were willing to go to such lengths.

d: A man’s close-fitting jacket; worn during the Renaissance
ety: From Middle English doublet, a borrowing from Old French doublet, from double, duble, doble + -et. Equivalent to double + -et (diminutive suffix)
s: He was a stout old gentleman, with a weather-beaten countenance; he wore a laced doublet, broad belt and hanger, high-crowned hat and feather, red stockings, and high-heeled shoes, with roses in them.

d: An evasion of the point of an argument by raising irrelevant distinctions or objections
ety: Origin uncertain. Possibly from quib (“quibble”, noun) + -le (diminutive ending). Quib is probably from Latin quibus (“in what respect? how?”), which appeared frequently in legal documents and came to be suggestive of the verbosity and petty argumentation found therein; or perhaps an alteration of quip. Alternatively, perhaps related to dialectal Dutch kwebbelen (“to speak quickly and continuously
s: He harped on his quibble about how the dark red paint should be described as carmine rather than burgundy.

d: Incapable of being repudiated or transferred to another
ety: Borrowed around 1645 from French inaliénable, from in- + aliénable (“alienable”), equivalent to in- + alienable.
s: An inalienable right is a right that cannot be given away nor taken away.

d: Unpleasantly and excessively suave or ingratiating in manner or speech
ety: From smarm + -y. Apparently coined by "B.R.L., of Brighton" with sense "saying treacly things which do not sound genuine" in a competition for neologisms in The Academy (London) published on 14 January 1899.
s: Starring a smarmy dog and scores of hapless flying wildfowl, Duck Hunt was the game that introduced many to the joys of the NES Zapper lightgun.

d: Naughtily or annoyingly playful
ety: From pixie, with ending as in titillated.
s: The melancholy beauty of Strachur and Inveraray was for me complicated by the agonies of first love; I was well and truly pixilated, and I soaked myself in the works of Niel Munroe and Maurice Walsh…

d: In the current fashion or style
ety: From mode + -ish.
s: As we crossed Blackwell's Island a limousine passed us, driven by a white chauffeur, in which sat three modish negroes, two bucks and a girl.

d: An elaborate analytical or explanatory essay or discussion
ety: Borrowed from French disquisition (“disquisition”), from Latin disquīsītiō (“inquiry, investigation”), from disquīrō (“to investigate”) (from dis- (prefix meaning ‘apart, asunder’) + quaerō (“to look for, seek; to inquire, question”)) + -tiō (suffix forming nouns relating to an action or the result of an action).
s: Everett’s novels make abundant use of language games, conceits and disquisitions.

d: Unequivocally detestable
ety: From Middle English odious, from Old French odieus, from Latin odiōsus, from odium (“hate”).
s: Scrubbing the toilets in the bar at the end of a Saturday night is an odious task.

d: A large metal or pottery vessel with a handle and spout; used to hold alcoholic beverages (usually wine)
ety: From Middle English flagon, flakon [and other forms], from Middle French flacon, Old French flacon, flascon (“flask”) (modern French flacon (“vial”)), from Medieval Latin flascōnem, the accusative singular of Late Latin flascō (“bottle; glass or earthenware vessel for wine; portable barrel”), from Frankish *flaska (“bottle; flask”), from Proto-Germanic *flaskǭ (“bottle; flask; vessel covered with
s: "He's got a venison pastry and a flagon of sack in that cupboard behind him."

d: Without limits in extent or size or quantity
ety: From il- + limitable.
s: That everlasting quest for new frontiers continues today as earthlings burst terrestrial bonds and begin the endless voyage beyond planet and galaxy into the illimitable dark.

d: A natural disposition to fight
ety: From bellicose + -osity.
s: The timing is intriguing too. Before this news North Korea was all bellicosity and bluster.

d: A minor parish official who serves a ceremonial function
ety: From Middle English bedel, bidel, from Old English bydel (“warrant officer, apparitor”), from Proto-West Germanic *budil, from Proto-Germanic *budilaz (“herald”), equivalent to bid + -le. Cognate with Dutch beul, German Büttel. More at bid.
s: His face expressed horror and indignation. Instinct rather than reason came to my help; he was a Beadle; I was a woman.

d: Someone excellent of their kind
ety: From crack (“highly skilled, excellent”) + -er + jack (“man”).
s: "Here, here's the popcorn man," Sid said as a vendor passed, pushing a cart. Sid bought a package of crackerjack and opened it while Mickey jumped up and down, unable to wait.

d: A figure consisting of three stylized human arms or legs (or three bent lines) radiating from a center
ety: Circa 1885, alongside triskeles (c. 1880), from French triskèle (1835).
s: Both materials have the triskele geometry.

d: Glazed earthenware decorated with opaque colors
ety: Borrowed from French faïence, named after the city of Faenza, Italy, where it was made in the 16th century.
s: The smile, you see, is perfect—wonderful / As mere Faience! a table ornament / To suit the richest mounting.

d: A child’s tight-fitting cap; often ties under the chin
ety: From French béguin. Compare beguine.
s: An old woman's biggin for a nightcap.

d: A servant employed to do a variety of jobs
ety: Ellipsis of domine fac totum, dominus fac totum /dominus factotum (“absolute ruler; head servant”), from Medieval Latin domine fac tōtum (“O Lord, do everything”), also with substition of nominative dominus for vocative domine.
s: Biden’s and Bush’s factotums had to walk their statements quickly back, emphasizing that U.S. policy had not changed.

d: Of great mass; huge and bulky
ety: From French Gargantua, a giant with a very large appetite in Rabelais's The Inestimable Life of Gargantua. Rabelais derived Gargantua from the Portuguese and Spanish garganta (“throat”).
s: Boxy and unrefined, the Hummer embodied an outlandishly masculine aesthetic that seemed to almost revel in its gargantuan fuel consumption.

d: Alternative terms for gallows
ety: From Middle English gibet, from Old French gibet (French gibet), either from Frankish *gibb (“forked stick”) or from Latin gibbus (“hunchbacked”).
s: Why, your cavalier is a rebel—an exile, whose property is confiscated, and for whose neck the gibbet stands prepared!

d: An outcome (good or bad) that is well deserved
ety: From come up (“to appear before a judge”) + -ance.
s: More comeuppance comes when the two play on the national team eight years later.

d: A scolding nagging bad-tempered woman
ety: The noun is derived from Termagant (“fictitious deity with a violent temperament represented as being worshipped by Muslims or other non-Christians”), from Middle English Termagaunt (“fictitious deity represented as being worshipped by Muslims; any pagan god”), from Anglo-Norman Tervagant, Tervagaunt, Tervagan, and Old French Tervagant, Tervagan (possibly with the addition of Anglo-Norman -aunt, O
s: The name of Xanthippe, the wife of Socrates, has become proverbial for a termagant.

d: Unpleasantly loud and harsh
ety: Borrowed from Latin raucus (“hoarse, husky, raucous”).
s: At night, raucous ruckus took place in the swamp.

d: The total output of a writer or artist (or a substantial part of it)
ety: From French œuvre, from Old French uevre, from Latin opera (plural of Latin opus), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ep- (“work”). Doublet of opera, opus, and ure.
s: Let’s “fictionalize” Foucault’s life by turning it into a biographical account of Foucault and his oeuvre or work.

d: A diplomat who is fully authorized to represent his or her government
ety: From Medieval Latin plēnipotentiārius (“having full power”), Late Latin plēnipotēns, from plēnus (“full”) + potēns (“mighty, powerful”).
s: None but the like-minded can come plenipotentiary to our court.

d: An ornamental jeweled headdress signifying sovereignty
ety: From Middle English diademe, dyademe, from Old French diademe, from Latin diadēma, from Ancient Greek διάδημα (diádēma, “band, especially worn around a tiara”), from διαδέω (diadéō, “bind around”).
s: The Apollon wing of the Louvre has a set of historic crowns, diadems and sovereign jewellery.

d: A style that involves indirect ways of expressing things
ety: From Latin circumlocūtiō (“the act of speaking around; circumlocution, periphrasis”). By surface analysis, circum- (“around”) + locution (“talk”), thus "getting around (a problem) in speaking or writing". Probably a calque of Ancient Greek περίφρασις (períphrasis, “periphrasis”).
s: A technical word, such as hyperkalemia or hypoallergenic, can be glossed for general audiences with a circumlocution, such as "high potassium level" or "less likely to cause allergies" (respectively).
